new_statements.rule_in_words: Speece treats stress as an underlying (lexical) property of multisyllabic nominals — it must be written in their underlying forms — while in all other words (verbals, monosyllables, etc.) it is 'predictable'; the rule that predicts it is never formulated anywhere in the 139 pages. Surface transcriptions show nominals with initial, penultimate and final stress (['ema] 'moon', [u'Fau?wu?] 'ashes', [onda'bi?] 'pig', [wa'ta?] 'board'), and verb derivations with a 'stress assignment' step (e.g. /PePfTaot/ -> [paba'ta?owu] 'they'll die', /Toamfant/ -> [fa?'ma?ana] 'I'll remove'), i.e. antepenultimate in those five- and four-syllable verb forms, but the article states no such rule. The language also has a word tone system (referred to Speece & Speece 1981/82 MS; dictionary entries carry tone-class labels like [L'H]).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated beyond the nominal/other split; extensive idiolectal variation is noted for segments, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (underlying and surface word forms; verbals vs nominals). Speece also classes glottal stop as a syllable-level suprasegmental and notes 'English stress.. is perceived as a degree of intensity' when arguing that glottal stop is not stress-like. Lloyd 1973: 87-88 (family survey) says tone and stress are 'combined in a complex unit' tied to the grammatical stem and that Angan languages other than Angaataha are 'intonation languages'.
new_statements.identity_note: Source language name is 'Angave' (SIL spelling) = Ankave anka1246 [aak]; Speece's data come from the Swanson/Mbwei headwaters (Angai, Winoyit, Wiokwa, Bu'u, Ikwundi, Onapai ridges) with prolific idiolectal variation and no clear lect boundaries (Speece 1988: 3). No separate dialect glottocodes.

sources.note: Whole article is a phonology (139 pp.). Only explicit stress statement is footnote 3, p. 131: stress is marked on all surface forms but underlyingly only on multisyllabic nominals, 'as elsewhere it is predictable'; tone not marked, word tone system described in Speece & Speece (MS). No positional stress rule is ever formulated; VOWEL REDUCTION (350), p. 105, refers to 'a syllable that precedes the stressed syllable by two' in verbals and derivation (351) has a 'stress assignment' step; STRIDENCY (211), p. 64, is conditioned by stressed syllables. sources.note: Sec. 2.121 'Phonology' of Ankave (pp. 81-82) lists consonants/vowels from a survey wordlist, nothing on stress. Family-level remark (sec. 2.152, pp. 87-88): 'Tone and stress are combined in a complex unit which usually occurs in connection with the grammatical stem. Angaataha, with four tonemes, is noticeably different from the other Angan languages. In Angaataha stress is also linked to high tone. Thus Angaataha is like a "tone language" and the others are more "intonation languages"'; also 'Vowels tend to be slightly longer in stressed syllables or in short words'.
